description: Salut ! Hello ! Nous sommes trois étudiants en science planétaire, nous avons des spécialités en language de programmation appliquée aux images satellites, géologie lunaire et terrestre, outils de la géomatique. Deux d'entre nous ont déjà fait des "Geologic field trip (USA et Europe)" et (planteray science hackathon). Nous sommes deux en présentiel à Sherbrooke, un à distance (France). On accepte avec une spécialité ingénierie spatiale/aéronautique ; en IA.
summary: Traditional analog sites have typically been chosen by NASA by heritage or reputation, i. e. the organization has been using the same list of locations for sixty years, picked for specific geologies, before they had settled on the lunar South Pole. For this challenge, we took criteria from NASA’s Artemis III Science Definition Team report. We adapted them, then applied a script to Google Earth Engine, which in turn divided the Earth’s map into 2.46 million cells, with each cell having a spatial resolution of 10 km. We excluded the 32 known analog and training sites, and 50 km around each, so every result is a new candidate, using the Analytic Hierarchy Process. The outcome is 18,516 new candidate sites on six continents, 202 of them scoring above 0.70. The best lie at the Arctic Circle, near 66° N. The classic lunar analogs rank at the 30th to 40th percentile, because they were chosen for their rocks. No single place fits all criteria, as no site on Earth compares perfectly to the Moon. The practical answer is a network of complementary rehearsal sites, each carrying a critical part of the mission.
details:
What it is

A web app that answers a practical question: where on Earth should we go to rehearse a given part of the Artemis Moon mission? You pick what you want to test, and the app returns the sites that match, each with its score, its measurements, what it reproduces and what it does not. Behind it is a reproducible pipeline that scored every 10 km square of Earth’s land against the Artemis III landing criteria.

How it works

Seven steps, each a script in the repository.

  1. The Moon fingerprint. We read the NASA LRO LOLA south-pole elevation model at 120 m and measure Shackleton crater’s terrain: slope, roughness, relief. That becomes the profile Earth is compared against, measured rather than estimated.
  2. Earth features. Google Earth Engine computes 14 features for each of the 2.46 million 10 km squares: slope, roughness, relief, trafficable ground within 2, 10 and 50 km, permafrost class, sand content, vegetation and aridity.
  3. Scoring. Each criterion scores 0 to 1, and is met at 0.70. A square must pass three hard constraints first: no vegetation (annual maximum NDVI below 0.2), some passable ground (at least 5% within 2 km), and at least half ice-free land. Weights come from the Artemis priorities through the Analytic Hierarchy Process: illumination 0.467, water ice 0.277, terrain and mobility 0.160, regolith and soil 0.095. Touching squares of the same tier form a site of at most 50 km, the pressurised-rover range the report gives.
  4. Validation. We used the 32 known analog and training sites, and the 50 km around each that wereexcluded from the results to validate the method; they are not discoveries. 
  5. Dossiers. The best sites are re-measured at 120 m from the ESA Copernicus DEM, with a full year of Sun positions and real cast shadows, giving the share of available sunlight each square metre receives.
  6. The executive summary is generated from the results, so no number is typed by hand.

What we found

Eighteen thousand and five hundred and sixteen new candidate sites on six continents, with two hundred and two of them scoring above 0.70; none are within 50 km of a known analog.

The best are at the Arctic Circle: MOON-0001 in West Greenland (66.43 N, 49.54 W, score 0.86), MOON-0002 on Baffin Island (0.85), MOON-0011 in East Greenland near Tasiilaq (0.84). They share what the Artemis report searches for: the Sun below 10 degrees for about 107 days a year, ground frozen from the surface, and 90% or more of the land passable within 10 km.

No single place has everything, and no site reaches Tier 1. The best site differs by criterion: low Sun on Baffin Island, Shackleton-like slopes and relief on the Andean Altiplano, sandy regolith in the Taklamakan and the Sahara, flat frozen ground in the New Siberian Islands. The practical answer is a network of complementary rehearsal sites.

How we know it holds

The classic lunar analogs rank at the 30th to 40th percentile on this profile (Mauna Kea, Meteor Crater, Mistastin), while the high-latitude ones rank higher (McMurdo Dry Valleys, 73rd). That is not a failure of the method: those sites were initially chosen for their rocks, and this processing chain measures the surface, not the geology. We report it rather than hide it.

The ranking is stable. Moving any weight by 20% keeps 96 to 100 of the top 100 squares.

What it is for

A field campaign to look for analog sites without a road plan, or a field chosen based on faulty criteria will cost time and money to the company. The app gives the mission planner a ranked, auditable shortlist for a stated purpose, as well as the proper data behind every number.

Where this goes next

The tool is built; what it enables is larger than what we could finish in a weekend.

Mars. The same processing chain, against NASA’s 47 candidate human Exploration Zones. The pipeline is already written to take a second target profile.

Mission itineraries. A campaign rarely tests one thing. The next version takes a list of what a team needs to test — mineralogy, power equipment, mobility, drilling — and returns a route: a small set of sites that together cover everything, ordered so the travel between them is as short as possible, with what each stop can and cannot deliver. Choosing a site based on a pre-planned itinerary is not the same as planning a proespecting campaign.

Robotic-focused vs human-focused missions. The constraints are not the same. A rover needs trafficable ground and a power budget; a crew needs access, safety and logistics. Splitting the scoring into two profiles would let the same map serve both, instead of averaging their needs into one compromise.

A feedback loop with the field. We allow users to provide useful reviews after their field experiences to improve the scores. The app already lets someone who has visited a site say whether the data matched the ground, criterion by criterion. The next step is to feed those reviews back into the scores, that is because confirming the site on the ground is always better than relying only on satellite data. The map then improves from two directions at once, satellite measurement and field experience, rather than from calculation alone.

Finer data. At 10 km, a square averages away the feature a team would actually drive to. With higher-resolution elevation and surface data, and the compute to run it, the same method would resolve individual landforms instead of landscapes, and the dossiers would answer “where exactly do we set up” rather than “which region.”

What it cannot do

Earth cannot reproduce gravity, vacuum or radiation. Lunar cold traps are near 110 K; the coldest temperature measured on Earth is about 184 K. Squares are 10 km, so small features are averaged out, and Antarctica’s ice-free oases are smaller than one square. Near ice-sheet edges the frozen-ground class comes from a 9 km soil model and needs a field check. Geology and mineralogy are not measured yet. Every site needs a visit before use.

Software and platforms

Python 3.12, Google Earth Engine, pandas, GeoPandas, rasterio, matplotlib, pytest. The whole chain runs on synthetic data in about 20 seconds as a test. Code, data tables and method are public under the MIT licence.

NASA Data

High-Resolution LOLA Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites (Barker et al. 2021). Read at 120 m to measure the terrain of Shackleton crater, which becomes the Artemis III south pole profile every Earth square is compared against (scripts/00_moon_fingerprint.py).

MOD13A2.061 Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day Global 1km (Didan, Kamel. (2021). MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 Global 1km SIN Grid V061. NASA Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center. ). Annual maximum NDVI per 10 km square. Used as a hard constraint: the Moon has no vegetation, so a square with NDVI above 0.2 is removed before scoring.

MCD12Q1.061 MODIS Land Cover Type Yearly Global 500m (Friedl, Mark, & Sulla-Menashe, Damien. (2022). MODIS/Terra+Aqua Land Cover Type Yearly L3 Global 500m SIN Grid V061 [Data set]. NASA Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center. ).The Terra and Aqua combined Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Land Cover Type (MCD12Q1) Version 6.1 data product provides global land cover types at yearly intervals. The MCD12Q1 Version 6.1 data product is derived using supervised classifications of MODIS Terra and Aqua reflectance data.  

Artemis III Science Definition Team Report (NASA, 2020). The source of the criteria themselves. Its priorities set our weights, and its quantified figures became the Earth measurements we compute: sites lit more than 200 days a year, the Shackleton rim lit more than 90% of the year, no point on the Moon permanently lit, the 2 km walk-back range, the ice-stability depth classes, and the 50 km pressurised-rover range that sets our maximum site size.

Global 1-km Gridded Thickness of Soil, Regolith, and Sedimentary Deposit Layers (Pelletier, J. D., Broxton, P. D., Hazenberg, P., Zeng, X., Troch, P. A., Niu, G., Williams, Z. C., Brunke, M. A., & Gochis, D. (2016). Global 1-km Gridded Thickness of Soil, Regolith, and Sedimentary Deposit Layers (Version 1). ORNL Distributed Active Archive Center. ).

All of it open, and all of it cited in the repository README.

Space Agency Partner & Other Data

ESA (European Space Agency), through the Copernicus programme

Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (2024_1): Global 30m Digital Elevation Model. (https://doi.org/10.5270/ESA-c5d3d65). The Copernicus DEM is a Digital Surface Model (DSM) that represents the surface of the Earth including buildings, infrastructure and vegetation. The Copernicus DEM is provided in 3 different instances: EEA-10, GLO-30 and GLO-90.

ECMWF and the Copernicus Climate Change Service

ERA5-Land Monthly Aggregated - ECMWF Climate Reanalysis (DOI: 10.24381/cds.68d2bb30). ERA5-Land is a reanalysis dataset providing a consistent view of the evolution of land variables over several decades at an enhanced resolution compared to ERA5.

Other open data

  • OpenLandMap Sand Content (Tomislav Hengl. (2018). Sand content in % (kg / kg) at 6 standard depths (0, 10, 30, 60, 100 and 200 cm) at 250 m resolution (Version v0.2) [Dataset].). Sand content in % (kg / kg) at 6 standard depths (0, 10, 30, 60, 100 and 200 cm) at 250 m resolution. Based on machine learning predictions from global compilation of soil profiles and samples. Processing steps are described in detail here. Antarctica is not included.
  • TerraClimate: Monthly Climate and Climatic Water Balance for Global Terrestrial Surfaces, University of Idaho (Abatzoglou, J.T., S.Z. Dobrowski, S.A. Parks, K.C. Hegewisch, 2018, Terraclimate, a high-resolution global dataset of monthly climate and climatic water balance from 1958-2015, Scientific Data, ), for aridity.
  • Natural Earth 1:10m lakes and reservoirs, removed because an elevation model shows a lake as flat bare ground; dry salt lakes such as Lake Eyre are kept.
  • Sources des basemap utilisées pour le site internet : Google, Bing, Esri.

Others

All code, text and figures in this submission are the team’s own work, released under the MIT licence. No copyrighted images are used.

Use of Artificial Intelligence- AI assistance

We used Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, as a coding and writing assistant during the hackathon.

What the team did: the project idea and research question; the choice of a global similarity ranking; the selection of the Artemis III criteria and how to measure them on Earth; all final decisions on thresholds, weights, site size and the list of known analogs to exclude; running the pipeline on Google Earth Engine and our own computers; checking the results; and the final text.

What Claude helped with: writing and debugging the Python code (the Earth Engine exports, scoring, validation, shadow modelling, the book and executive-summary generators, and the Streamlit app); suggesting data-quality checks that we then adopted (removing lakes, ice sheets, and squares that are half ice and half water); and drafting documentation and submission text, which we edited.

Every AI-assisted script starts with the line "Written with assistance from Claude (Anthropic); reviewed by the team." No AI-generated images, video or audio are used. All results come from running the code on the data listed above.
